title: E.H. Taylor Jr. and the Bottled-in-Bond Act, 1897
summary: Frankfort distiller E.H. Taylor Jr. rebuilt Kentucky whiskey’s reputation and helped push the Bottled-in-Bond Act, signed on March 3, 1897.
bodyMarkdown:
Colonel [Edmund Haynes Taylor Jr.](/people/#e-h-taylor-jr) (1830–1923) was born in Columbia, Kentucky, and raised in Frankfort. He was a grandnephew of President [Zachary Taylor](/people/#zachary-taylor). He started out in banking, and he learned the whiskey trade from the money side before he ever ran a still.

After the Civil War, Taylor set out to make Kentucky whiskey that people could trust. In 1869 he bought a small distillery near Frankfort and rebuilt it as the O.F.C., for Old Fire Copper, with new equipment and careful methods. That plant grew into what is now Buffalo Trace. In 1887 he built the Old Taylor Distillery on Glenn's Creek in Woodford County, with a stone castle, a sunken garden, and a springhouse meant to show visitors that his whiskey was made right.

The trade had a problem. Many sellers, called rectifiers, bought cheap grain alcohol and colored and flavored it with caramel, tobacco, prune juice, or worse. They sold it as Kentucky bourbon. Honest distillers lost sales, and buyers had no way to tell what they were getting.

Taylor worked with Treasury Secretary [John G. Carlisle](/people/#john-g-carlisle), a Kentuckian, to fix that. The result was the [Bottled-in-Bond Act](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bottled_in_bond), signed March 3, 1897. To carry the bond label, a spirit had to be made by one distiller at one distillery in one season. It had to age at least four years in a federally bonded warehouse, under government lock. It had to be bottled at 100 proof with nothing added but water. A green government stamp sealed each bottle.

It was one of the nation's first consumer-protection laws, nine years before the Pure Food and Drug Act. The bond stamp told buyers that what was inside was real straight whiskey.

Taylor also served as mayor of Frankfort for many years and in the state legislature. He kept making whiskey until Prohibition loomed, and died in 1923.

## Kentucky today

Buffalo Trace Distillery in Frankfort still sells an E.H. Taylor Jr. line. The Old Taylor castle on Glenn's Creek was restored and reopened as the Castle & Key distillery. Bottled-in-bond whiskey is still made under the same basic rules.
